title: The Sacrifice of the New Creation - 3

content:
In our recent studies we have seen the lamb, the ram, and the young bull, and how the offering must rise to match the greatness of the sacrifice. We saw that with each animal came fine flour, olive oil, and wine, and that all three had to increase together. Now let us look at these three accompanying offerings one by one, and ask a very practical question about each: how do we actually give it to God? Today we begin with the fine flour, which speaks of our character, and we will see five ways in which we bring each of this offering to Yahweh.

First, we give our character through the sifting of daily trials. It is important to understand what fine flour really is. It does not begin as fine flour. It begins as grain, and it must be ground and sifted again and again until it becomes pure and smooth. And this is exactly how our character is offered to God. We do not become refined merely by claiming that we are refined. We become refined by submitting to the grinding and the repeated sifting that trials produce. James writes, "When troubles of any kind come your way, consider it an opportunity for great joy. For you know that when your faith is tested, your endurance has a chance to grow. So let it grow, for when your endurance is fully developed, you will be perfect and complete, needing nothing" (James 1:2-4). We do not enjoy the grinding. But we must trust that the very process we would avoid is the process that makes the flour fine. When we submit to the trial instead of resisting it, we are bringing Yahweh the offering of a refined character.

Second, we give consistency, not performance. Notice that fine flour has no lumps. It is even and the same all the way through. And this teaches us that the offering of our character must have no lumps either, no hidden pockets of a different life. We must show the same patience at home that we show in the meeting house. We must keep the same integrity in private that we display in public. The New Creation offering cannot be a double life, smooth and pleasant where others can see, but coarse and unrefined where no one is watching. A life that is one thing before the brethren and another thing behind closed doors is a lumpy offering. Yahweh asks for flour that is fine all the way through,
a character that is consistent whether or not anyone is watching, because He Himself is always watching.

Third, we give an increasing quantity as our sight of Christ increases. We remember from the offerings that the flour rose from one-tenth of an ephah for the lamb, to two-tenths for the ram, to three-tenths for the young bull.

A shallow view of the sacrifice of Christ produces only a lamb-sized offering of character. But a deep view of that same sacrifice demands the bull-sized measure. This means our growth in doctrine and understanding must actually produce a growth in refinement. It is not enough to learn more and more about Christ while our character stays exactly where it was. As we see more of what He gave for us, we must bring more of a refined life in return. Knowledge that does not deepen our character has failed to do its work. The more clearly we see the cross, the finer our flour must become.

Fourth, we give it willingly, and as an ongoing offering, not as a finished product. The flour for the offering was brought fresh each time. It was not stored up from a past season and set aside as though the worshipper had already done enough. And this teaches us something searching. Yesterday's refinement does not excuse today's offering. We cannot point back to the character we showed a year ago, or to a trial we passed through long ago, and imagine that we no longer need to bring the offering today. Each day calls for fresh flour. The patience we showed last week does not cover the impatience of this morning. The New Creation brings the offering of character freshly, again and again, willingly and without growing tired of it, because it is an ongoing offering and not a task once completed and then forgotten.

Fifth, we give what has been beaten, not what came easily. The fine flour of the offering, called Soleth, was flour that had truly passed through the beating and the grinding. It was not ordinary flour that had been quickly gathered. There is another Hebrew word, qemach, which simply means ordinary meal. And here is the searching truth: we cannot skip the hammering and still bring Soleth. Whatever character we offer to God must have actually passed through testing, or it is not the offering flour at all, but only ordinary meal. A gentleness that has never been tested by provocation, a patience that has never been stretched by delay, a faith that has never been tried by hardship, is qemach and not Soleth. It is the ordinary, not the offering. Yahweh receives the character that has been beaten fine through real testing, the character that has been proven in the mill of daily life. So let us not despise the hammering, for it is the very thing that turns ordinary meal into an offering fit for the altar. In our next study, Yahweh willing, we will look at the olive oil, and how we give ourselves to be saturated and filled with the Spirit of God.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,
We bring You the offering of our character, and we ask You to make our flour fine.

Help us not to resist the sifting of trials, but to trust the process that refines us.

Take the lumps from our lives, that we may be the same in private as we are in public.

As our sight of Christ grows, let our refinement grow to match it, fresh each new day.

And teach us not to despise the beating, for it turns ordinary meal into an offering.

"Consider it an opportunity for great joy when troubles of any kind come your way." James 1:2

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
